Azara (Akodon azarae) is a small sigmodontine rodent endemic to the grasslands and agricultural margins of the southern cone of South America, where it occupies a key ecological role as a primary consumer in disturbed habitats. Neonates of this species emerge from the birth canal weighing approximately 2.4 grams [Wwb = approximately 2.4 grams], a modest initial mass characteristic of altricial murid rodents that require an extended period of maternal care, and notably lower than the neonatal weights reported for some larger-bodied congeners in the genus Akodon. This low birth weight is consistent with the general pattern observed among small-bodied rodents, where energetic constraints on gestation lead to relatively undeveloped young at parturition. The pronounced altriciality of the newborn pups necessitates a substantial investment in lactation and brooding by the female during the critical first weeks of life, a phase during which the young are entirely dependent on the mother for thermoregulation and nutrition. Studies of captive colonies have provided detailed data on the early life history of this species, allowing for precise measurement of developmental milestones under controlled thermal conditions that approximate the species' normothermic body temperature.

Under the stable thermal conditions typical of a normothermic and active adult, approximately 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C], the gestation period of Akodon azarae has been measured at 22.7 days [tg = 22.7 days]. This relatively brief intrauterine development, lasting just over three weeks, is typical for a rodent of this body size and reflects the fast-paced life history strategy common to many small mammals inhabiting unpredictable environments, where rapid population turnover is an adaptive response to high predation pressure and fluctuating resource availability. Following a gestation that is short even by murid standards, the female gives birth to a litter of altricial young. The completion of the gestation period at this temperature underscores the efficiency of the species' reproductive physiology under baseline metabolic conditions, as the internal environment of the mother remains tightly regulated. This specific thermal context is crucial, as the rate of foetal development in small endotherms is tightly coupled to maternal metabolic rate, which in turn depends on the maintenance of a high and stable core body temperature.

The weaning of the altricial young represents a pivotal transition from nutritional dependence to independent foraging. In Akodon azarae, the time since birth at weaning has been documented as 14.5 days [tx = 14.5 days] at a body temperature of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C]. This remarkably early weaning age underscores a life-history strategy that prioritizes rapid offspring independence, likely an adaptation to seasonal resource pulses in its native Pampean grassland habitat. Once weaned, the juvenile is capable of consuming solid food but remains vulnerable to predation and must continue rapid somatic growth. The efficient transfer of maternal antibodies through milk during this brief suckling period is critical for neonatal survival, as the pup's own immune system is just beginning to mature. This period also marks the start of intense growth that will carry the juvenile toward the next major developmental milestone.

Sexual maturation in female Azara grass mice occurs relatively early in life, consistent with their rapid life-history strategy. Specifically, the time since birth at puberty for females is 60 days [tp = 60 days] at a body temperature of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C]. This rapid attainment of reproductive capability allows females born early in the breeding season to contribute offspring to the same seasonal cohort, a critical factor driving population growth in these ephemeral grassland habitats. The onset of the first oestrous cycle at roughly two months of age enables a high intrinsic rate of population increase, although actual reproductive output is often constrained by food availability and density-dependent factors. This early puberty, combined with a brief gestation and quick weaning, allows the species to exhibit a multi-voltine breeding pattern across the austral spring and summer, with the potential for multiple overlapping generations within a single favorable year.

The overall pace of life in Akodon azarae is further illuminated by its maximum reproductive rate and ultimate body size. Under the same normothermic conditions of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C], females produce a typical litter size of 3.2 pups per litter [N_R_i = 3.2 pups per litter], a fecundity that is moderate among small murids but consistent with the species' rapid life history. The frequency with which females can produce these litters over the course of a year is substantial; available data suggest they achieve approximately 2 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 2 litters per year], allowing for multiple cohorts within a single breeding season. In terms of somatic growth, the ultimate wet weight of adult individuals stabilizes around 26 grams [Wwi = around 26 grams], though field records show a considerable intraspecific range of 10 to 45 grams depending on local resource conditions and population density, reflecting phenotypic plasticity in response to environmental quality. Finally, the species' maximum lifespan has been recorded as roughly one year [am = roughly one year] at 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C], a short longevity that forces a high reproductive investment in a brief window of opportunity characteristic of many small r-selected grassland rodents inhabiting temporally variable environments.
